title: The Cold War, decolonization and the world since 1990
note: After 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union led rival blocs in a Cold War of alliances, arms races and proxy wars, while most colonies in Asia and Africa won independence. The Soviet bloc collapsed between 1989 and 1991, opening an era of globalization, new conflicts and shared global problems.

read.title: A divided world and after
text: World War II left two superpowers. The United States and its allies favored capitalism and elected governments; the Soviet Union installed communist regimes across Eastern Europe. Churchill warned of an iron curtain dividing the continent. The United States answered with containment: the Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan aid and the NATO alliance. The Soviets formed the Warsaw Pact. Both sides built nuclear arsenals large enough to destroy each other, so they rarely fought directly. Instead the Cold War turned hot in Korea and Vietnam, and it came close to nuclear war over Cuba in 1962.

At the same time, empires weakened by the war could no longer hold their colonies. India and Pakistan won independence in 1947, Ghana in 1957, and dozens of African states by the mid-1960s, some peacefully and some, like Algeria, after long wars. Many new nations refused to join either bloc and formed the Non-Aligned Movement.

In the 1980s Mikhail Gorbachev tried to reform the Soviet system through openness and restructuring. When Eastern Europeans demanded freedom in 1989, he did not send tanks, and the Berlin Wall fell. The Soviet Union itself dissolved in 1991. The world that followed was more connected by trade and technology but faced terrorism, regional wars and climate change.
